note: Benchmark footage. The videos are never committed; this file describes them so that a clip can be added, calibrated and asserted on without editing test code. See README.md in this folder.

clips.title: Lin Dan, four points, German Open
clips.source: Broadcast footage from YouTube. Third party: kept locally, never committed or redistributed.
clips.view: behind the baseline, raised to about eye level, slightly off centre
clips.racket_hands_note: Read by eye from full-resolution crops at the contacts on 2026-09-05: the near player's racket goes up on his right (frames 101, 202, 343); the far player holds it in the hand on camera-right seen from the front, his left (frames 148, 395, 425, 455). The far player is the left-hander, Lin Dan. Detecting the far player as a left-hander did not raise his contact count (16 -> 13): his misses are prominence failures on a small, foreshortened swing, not the wrong arm.
clips.multi_point_note: Described as a single rally until 2026-09-05, and it is not one. This is a 40 s crop of lindan_source, whose between-point intervals are already cut, so it holds four points separated by two to six seconds of walking back and serving -- visible at frames 640 to 740, where both players stand at rest. Clip segmentation finds four stretches of play (9.4, 10.5, 3.3 and 5.9 s) and bouts take their boundaries from it.
guards: the tracker stays on the player and not on the seated line judge
an eye-level camera is diagnosed rather than blamed on the clicked points
bouts cut the four points apart rather than merging them into one bout carrying 96 m
a clip whose dead time is already cut reports no work-to-rest figure
moves are counted per trip to a corner, not per run of fast frames
the split-step signal survives the perspective drift
the opponent is tracked on his own side of the net, and neither the umpire on his chair nor the spectator above the far baseline takes his place
the rally chain finds contacts on both sides, asks who won rather than guessing, and states no result
clips.click_note: the near player's torso in the first frame, for the tracking click

court.note: The nine intersections of three detected sidelines (left doubles, left singles, centre) with three detected cross lines (baseline, doubles long service, short service), each line least-squares fitted to its own painted pixels. Reprojection error 0.35 cm, and it lands on every painted line at 0.0 px median, including the two right-hand sidelines it never saw and extrapolates. Hand-clicked points were tried and made it worse: adding the net-post bases read off a zoomed frame took the fit from 0.4 cm to 14 cm, because a post stands on a base plate and the visible bottom of the post is not the floor.

clips.post_tops_note: Clicked, and deliberately expected to fail: the camera sits near the 1.55 m post height, so the post tops are within a few pixels of the ground plane's horizon and map hundreds of metres up the court.

clips.source: The user's own screen recording of a match seen from behind.
guards: takeoff and landing are suggested within six frames of the truth
the export pack survives real footage end to end
the frame index stays exact on a variable-frame-rate clip

events.note: airborne about frames 207 to 228, verified by eye

clips.title: Two minutes of jump smashes, phone on a tripod
guards: a raw recording with a long rest in it is cut into play and idle where a person would cut it
a feeding drill is cut at its pauses between feeds, which are the length of a walk-back between points on match footage, and nowhere else: a few stretches, not a piece per smash
an unedited recording is not accused of having had its intervals cut: its rests run from 0 to 21.7 s, and the longest is what proves nobody edited it

states.note: By eye from a contact sheet at three-second steps. Two people walk on and talk close to the lens until about 15 s, stand talking at the far end until about 36 s, then one runs a jump-smash drill fed from the far end until about 109 s, and they walk back toward the camera at the end. The walk-on and walk-off read as play to a motion threshold, because a person close to the lens moves more pixels than a distant player smashing does; that costs pose time and nothing else, so it is accepted rather than tuned away.

clips.note: Long enough to be the clip for anything that needs several rallies rather than one. Its rests are genuinely variable, which is what makes it the counter-example to lindan_source.

clips.title: Lin Dan, twelve minutes, German Open (the source lindan_rally was cut from)
clips.source: Broadcast footage from YouTube. Third party: kept locally, never committed or redistributed.
clips.view: behind the baseline, raised to about eye level, slightly off centre; one continuous locked-off camera throughout
clips.edited_note: The between-point intervals are cut: a point ends and the video cuts to the next serve, leaving only the two or three seconds of walking back and settling. This is ground truth from the user, not inferred.
guards: clip segmentation recovers 45 stretches of play with a median of 10.3 s, against a published men's singles rally of 8.8 +/- 2.0 s
the merge gap stays below the 2.7 s pre-serve pause: at 2.5 s this clip collapsed into 16 blobs of median 47.5 s
an edited clip is detected and its rests disowned: 45 rests clustered 1.5 to 2.5 s with a longest of 6.2 s, where any unedited recording eventually contains a real break
clips.note: Twelve minutes and 228 MB, so tests use a prefix rather than the whole thing; the first 3600 frames give 7 stretches at a 10.5 s median and are enough to pin the behaviour.

clips.title: Kento Momota v Lin Dan, quarter-final, a full broadcast (55 minutes)
clips.source: Broadcast footage from YouTube, added by the user on 2026-09-06. Third party: kept locally, never committed or redistributed.
clips.view: broadcast production: the main camera raised behind one end, with cuts to replays, close-ups, the crowd and graphics
guards: random access stays under a quarter of a second anywhere in the clip: reading frame 40000 in order took twenty seconds and a step backwards a minute, which is the black viewer the reader's seek exists to prevent

with the court calibrated, every frame of the main camera is told from every close-up, replay and crowd shot: the wide shot scores 0.87 to 0.91 of the court's lines and everything else 0.00 to 0.09, with nothing in between
the 29 points of game one come out as about that many stretches of the court being visible, at a rally-length median
without a calibration the clip is not split at all rather than split backwards: above ten camera cuts the motion threshold is inverted, and a wrong answer that looks right is worse than none
the shuttle itself is found, on frames whose positions were read off the picture by eye rather than taken from the detector's own output
the brightness gate keeps the shuttle inside the candidate cap: plain motion leaves it ranked as low as 37th of about forty blobs, and only twelve are kept

game_one.note: From the frame the players take their positions for the first serve (the 'Kento MOMOTA' name graphic is up at 426 s) to just after the last point of game one, read off the broadcast's own scoreboard: 0-1 at 490 s, 20-8 at 1500 s with a challenge at 1530 s, and the board gone by 1560 s. 28451 frames, 1138 s.

court.note: The four doubles corners, eyeballed to about twenty pixels and then slid until every painted line the calibration projects sits on painted pixels -- the mean squared distance from the projection to a white-line mask fell from 22.2 px to 0.22 px. Fitting to the lines rather than clicking matters here: a hand-clicked calibration of this clip scored 0.52 of the lines found and this one scores 0.90, which is the difference between a court test with a margin and one without. Four points, so the reprojection error is exactly zero by construction and says nothing; the line score is the measure. Taken on a game-two frame and it holds through game one, because the main camera is locked off and only the replay cameras move.

shuttle_truth.note: Shuttle positions read by eye off full-resolution crops on 2026-09-06, from two flights in the rally at frames 11290-11314: a descent into the near player, and the lift he answered with, which decelerates smoothly and stalls at its apex around frame 11316. The first ground truth for the shuttle anywhere in this repo, and the point of it is that a detection sitting on a shoe cannot pass a test against it by agreeing with itself. Frame 11297 is deliberately absent: the shuttle crosses a painted line there and could not be placed confidently by eye, so nothing asserts on it. Positions are the visible centroid, which sits about 7 px behind the cork at this scale (4.7 cm, against a flight scatter of 1.4 px): that offset is along the flight and cancels in direction and speed, which is why it is tolerable, and it is also why no landing point or apex height may be taken from these.

clips.note: The first full match with a real broadcast's cuts, replays and adverts, which the not-badminton path of the segmenter had never met, and 785 MB, so nothing here decodes the whole of it: the reader test seeks, the frame cache fills ahead only to its budget, and the segmentation tests take game one. Three games: game one runs 426 to 1556 s, the interval to about 1700 s, and the match ends near 3080 s with an outro from 3120 s. Segmented; not yet through tracking or the chain in the suite.

clips.title: Lee Yong Dae and Yoo Yeon-seong v Fu Haifeng and Zhang Nan, men's doubles, Denmark Open: selected points from two games
clips.source: Broadcast footage re-cut by a YouTube channel, added by the user on 2026-09-25. Third party: kept locally, never committed or redistributed.
clips.view: behind the near baseline, raised well above head height, slightly left of centre; one locked-off camera throughout, no replays or close-ups
clips.edited_note: Cut to points only, and to a selection of them: about 35 stretches for 82 points on the scoreboard, so the score jumps between consecutive stretches and the serve chain will find rallies missing. The cuts are hard cuts on a locked-off camera, so the whole picture barely changes across one: the mean absolute frame difference at a cut is 5 to 12 on a 0 to 255 scale against a median of 1.5, which is what a scene-signature test that expects a different picture on each side of a cut will miss.
clips.near_baseline_note: The near baseline lies below the bottom edge of the picture. The nearest painted line in frame is the near doubles long service line, 76 cm inside the baseline, so a near player standing on the baseline has his feet out of frame and no court position on those frames. Every court preset in the app starts from the near corners, so this clip cannot be calibrated by clicking in the UI; the calibration below was fitted to the painted lines.
guards: four people are tracked on real doubles footage, two on each side, and nobody is confused with the umpire on his chair or the spectators above the far baseline
the cuts between points on a locked-off camera are found as splices and end the stretches of play, where the whole-picture cut test found none of them and eight points were one 90 s stretch

the clicked partner keeps his tracker through crossings and cuts, read off the two near players' shoes, and the far pair, alike down to the shoes and too small to read, are marked unresolved rather than guessed between

identity_truth.note: The two Korean players wear identical shirts and shorts and different shoes, Lee red and Yoo yellow; the hue of the saturated pixels at each track's foot keypoints, smoothed over half a second, says which person each tracker is on, and the two near trackers show opposite colours on 4,641 to 5,131 of the 5,614 frames of game one depending on the run. Measured on 2026-09-25 over game one with four players: continuity alone swapped the two near trackers sixteen times, ten at crossings and six at the cuts between points, and the clicked player (Yoo) had his own tracker on 63% of the readable frames. With appearance re-settling the pair on chroma, part by part, as a streak of five verdicts on every clean frame, and no signature read under 200 px: four events, two of them the corrections, 98.7% of readable frames on Yoo, and the far pair unresolved on all 73 of their decisions.

game_one.note: Frames 0 to 5613, the Korean pair near. The scoreboard reads 0-0 at frame 0, 6-9 at frame 3000 and 13-21 with game two at 2-0 by frame 5700; the cut at 5614 is the change of ends.

game_two.note: Frames 5614 to 16469, the Chinese pair near. 13-3 and 21-1 at frame 6100, 13-16 and 21-14 at 12000, 23-23 at 16000, 23-25 at the end; the outro fades from frame 16470.

players.kit_note: Both Korean players in navy in game one and grey in game two, both Chinese players in red throughout: matching kit within each pair, so no colour signature separates partners on this clip.

clips.click_note: the near-left player's torso in the first frame (Yoo Yeon-seong, by the name on his shirt), for the tracking click

court.note: Fitted, not clicked, on a player-free median of 82 frames spread across the clip: from a rough start on the two doubles sidelines and the near long service line, the four court points were slid to minimise the squared distance from every projected line sample to the nearest thin bright pixel (tophat over grey, 11 px). The two near corners come out below the bottom edge of the picture and are recorded as such. Line share on the background 0.66 and on the first frame 0.61, lower than the Momota broadcast's 0.90 because at 720p the far court's lines are read through the net mesh; every frame of this clip is the wide shot, so the score has no close-ups to separate from.

clips.note: The first doubles footage in this repo. Each pair is in matching kit, which is the case a colour signature cannot help with, so it tests the honest path for partner identity first. Selected points, not a match, so the serve chain can be checked against the scoreboard at each serve but never across the gaps between stretches.
